Appendix A Definitions/Notations

We re-iterate the definitions considered in the main text and to be used subsequently for remaining parts of this Appendix.

  • •

    v→=(v1,v2,…,vn)\vec{v}=(v_{1},v_{2},\dots,v_{n}): A binary configuration of the nn visible units, where each viv_{i} is a binary variable taking values in {−1,1}\{-1,1\}. Each configuration represents a possible classical state of the graph G2G_{2} or the visible set of neurons of graph G1G_{1}. Unless otherwise specified, we shall sometimes omit the vector sign above and simply use v∈[0,⋯,2n−1]v\in[0,\cdots,2^{n}-1]. This is akin to representing the corresponding integer index for the configuration in binary (with -1 substituted by 0).

  • •

    𝕍={v→|v→∈{−1,1}n}\mathbb{V}=\{\vec{v}|\vec{v}\in\{-1,1\}^{n}\}. One must note |𝕍|=2n|\mathbb{V}|=2^{n}.

  • •

    ρv′v\rho^{v}_{v^{\prime}}: The matrix element of the state ρ⁡(X→)\rho(\vec{X}) corresponding to basis states vv and v′v^{\prime}. It represents the density matrix of the state.

    ρv′v(X→)∝exp(−β∑iaivi+∑iai∗vi′)∏j=1mΓj(v→,b→,W→)Γj(v→′,b∗→,W∗→)\displaystyle\rho^{v}_{v^{\prime}}(\vec{X})\propto exp\left({-\beta\sum_{i}a_{i}v_{i}+\sum_{i}a_{i}^{*}v_{i}^{\prime}}\right)\>\prod_{j=1}^{m}\Gamma_{j}(\vec{v},\vec{b},\vec{W})\>\Gamma_{j}(\vec{v}^{\prime},\vec{b^{*}},\vec{W^{*}}) (15)

    where, Γj​(v→,b→,W→)=cosh⁡[β⁡(bj+∑i=1nWi​j​vi)]\Gamma_{j}(\vec{v},\vec{b},\vec{W})=\cosh\left[\beta\left(b_{j}+\sum_{i=1}^{n}W_{ij}v_{i}\right)\right] and

    • –

      aia_{i}: A complex-valued parameter associated with the bias for the ii-th visible unit in the system.

    • –

      bjb_{j}: A complex-valued parameter associated with the bias for the jj-th hidden unit in the system.

    • –

      Wi​jW_{ij}: The weight (coupling) between the ii-th visible unit and jj-th hidden unit.

  • •

    X→\vec{X}: A shorthand representation for all the parameters (a→,b→,W→)(\vec{a},\vec{b},\vec{W}) that define the state ρ⁡(X→)\rho(\vec{X}). These include complex-valued parameters associated with interactions and biases in the network.

  • •

    β\beta: The inverse temperature parameter.

  • •

    Hvv′H_{v}^{v^{\prime}}: The Hamiltonian matrix element of the driver (system being studied) between state configurations vv and v′v^{\prime}.

  • •

    The diagonal elements, ρvv\rho^{v}_{v}, are real and satisfy the normalization condition ∑vρvv=1\sum_{v}\rho^{v}_{v}=1. They can be seen as a probability distribution.

    ρvv​(x→)\displaystyle\rho^{v}_{v}(\vec{x}) ∝\displaystyle\propto exp(−2β∑iRe(ai)vi)∏j=1m|cosh(bj+∑i=1nWi​jvi)|2\displaystyle exp\left({-2\beta\sum_{i}\rm{Re}(a_{i})v_{i}}\right)\>\prod_{j=1}^{m}\left|\cosh\left(b_{j}+\sum_{i=1}^{n}W_{ij}v_{i}\right)\right|^{2} (16)
  • •

    Eloc​(v)=∑v′ρv′v​Hvv′ρvvE_{\mathrm{loc}}(v)=\frac{\sum_{v^{\prime}}\rho_{v^{\prime}}^{v}H_{v}^{v^{\prime}}}{\rho^{v}_{v}}: The local energy of the driver for the configuration vv. It measures the effective energy associated with the state vv, computed by taking into account all the other configurations v′v^{\prime} to which it is connected via the Hamiltonian matrix element of the driver.

  • •

    ϕ⁡(v)\phi(v): The distribution that represents the state of the surrogate network. It is defined as

    ϕv→​(l→​(X→),J→​(X→))\displaystyle\phi_{\vec{v}}(\vec{l}(\vec{X}),\vec{J}(\vec{X})) ∝\displaystyle\propto e−β∑ili(X→)vi+∑i​jJi​j(X→)vivj\displaystyle e^{-\beta\sum_{i}l_{i}(\vec{X})v_{i}+\sum_{ij}J_{ij}(\vec{X})v_{i}v_{j}} (17)

    Here li∈(l→​(X→)CLOSEl_{i}\in(\vec{l}(\vec{X}) denotes the on-site field at each spin of the surrogate network G2G_{2} in main text and OPENJi​j​(X→)∈J→​(X→))J_{ij}(\vec{X})\in\vec{J}(\vec{X})) denotes the mutual coupling between a pair of spins of G2G_{2}. ϕ⁡(v)\phi(v) satisfies the normalization condition ∑vϕ⁡(v)=1\sum_{v}\phi(v)=1.

  • •

    κ⁡(v)\kappa(v): A configuration dependent pre-factor chosen to establish the equivalence between ρvv\rho_{v}^{v} and ϕ⁡(v)\phi(v), as defined above

    ρvv≈κ⁡(v)​ϕ​(v)\rho_{v}^{v}\approx\kappa(v)\phi(v)

Appendix B Proof of generality of factorization of probability distribution

For a given probability distribution P:𝕍→[0,1]P:\mathbb{V}\to[0,1], we wish to prove Theorem II.1 in the main text. But to do that we would first like to prove certain lemmas where the key quantities of interest will be :

  1. 1.

    Fa→(v→)=v1a1v2a2⋯vnan=∏iviaia→=(a1,a2….an)withai∈{0,1}andv→∈𝕍F_{\vec{a}}(\vec{v})=v_{1}^{a_{1}}v_{2}^{a_{2}}\cdots v_{n}^{a_{n}}=\prod_{i}v_{i}^{a_{i}}\>\>\>\vec{a}=(a_{1},a_{2}....a_{n})\>\>with\>\>a_{i}\in\{0,1\}\>\>and\>\>\vec{v}\>\>\in\mathbb{V}. Each entry represents an element of a monomial binary basis.

  2. 2.

    χ={Fa→​(v→)|a→∈{0,1}n}\chi=\{F_{\vec{a}}(\vec{v})|\vec{a}\in\{0,1\}^{n}\}

We first would like to establish that the set χ\chi can act as a basis for the space of functions f:𝕍→ℝf:\mathbb{V}\to\mathbb{R} . We show this in two different ways using the following lemmas

Lemma B.1.

(Approach 1: Orthogonality of Monomial basis) Let us define two vectors a→,b→∈{0,1}n\vec{a},\vec{b}\in\{0,1\}^{n} such that for the monomials we have

Fa→​(v→)\displaystyle F_{\vec{a}}(\vec{v}) =v1a1v2a2⋯vnan=∏inviai\displaystyle=v_{1}^{a_{1}}v_{2}^{a_{2}}\cdots v_{n}^{a_{n}}=\prod_{i}^{n}v_{i}^{a_{i}}
Fb→​(v→)\displaystyle F_{\vec{b}}(\vec{v}) =v1b1v2b2⋯vnbn=∏invibi\displaystyle=v_{1}^{b_{1}}v_{2}^{b_{2}}\cdots v_{n}^{b_{n}}=\prod_{i}^{n}v_{i}^{b_{i}}

Then, with respect to the inner product ⟨Fa→​(v→),Fb→​(v→)⟩=12n​∑v→∈VFa→​(v→)​Fb→​(v→)\langle F_{\vec{a}}(\vec{v}),F_{\vec{b}}(\vec{v})\rangle=\frac{1}{2^{n}}\sum_{\vec{v}\in V}F_{\vec{a}}(\vec{v})F_{\vec{b}}(\vec{v}), the monomials Fa→​(v→)F_{\vec{a}}(\vec{v}) and Fb→​(v→)F_{\vec{b}}(\vec{v}) are orthonormal i.e. ⟨Fa→​(v→),Fb→​(v→)⟩=0\langle F_{\vec{a}}(\vec{v}),F_{\vec{b}}(\vec{v})\rangle=0 if a→≠b→\vec{a}\neq\vec{b} and 1 otherwise .

Proof.

Since Fa→​(v→):𝕍→ℝF_{\vec{a}}(\vec{v}):\mathbb{V}\to\mathbb{R}, it is easy to show ⟨Fa→​(v→),Fb→​(v→)⟩\langle F_{\vec{a}}(\vec{v}),F_{\vec{b}}(\vec{v})\rangle satisfies all three axioms of usual inner-products (linearity, positive semi-definiteness when a→=b→\vec{a}=\vec{b} and symmetry), thus we straightaway compute the inner product between two monomials Fa→​(v→)F_{\vec{a}}(\vec{v}) and Fb→​(v→)F_{\vec{b}}(\vec{v}):

⟨Fa→​(v→),Fb→​(v→)⟩\displaystyle\langle F_{\vec{a}}(\vec{v}),F_{\vec{b}}(\vec{v})\rangle =12n​∑v→∈VFa→​(v→)​Fb→​(v→)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2^{n}}\sum_{\vec{v}\in V}F_{\vec{a}}(\vec{v})F_{\vec{b}}(\vec{v})
=12n∑v→∈V∏i=1nviai⊕2bi\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2^{n}}\sum_{\vec{v}\in V}\prod_{i=1}^{n}v_{i}^{a_{i}\oplus_{2}b_{i}}
=12n∑v1→∈{1,−1}∑v2→∈{1,−1}⋅⋅∑vn→∈{1,−1}∏i=1nviai⊕2bi\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2^{n}}\sum_{\vec{v_{1}}\in\{1,-1\}}\sum_{\vec{v_{2}}\in\{1,-1\}}\cdot\cdot\sum_{\vec{v_{n}}\in\{1,-1\}}\prod_{i=1}^{n}v_{i}^{a_{i}\oplus_{2}b_{i}}
=(12∑v1∈{1,−1}v1a1⊕2b1)(12∑v2∈{1,−1}v2a2⊕2b2)⋯(12∑vn∈{1,−1}vnan⊕2bn)\displaystyle=\left(\frac{1}{2}\sum_{v_{1}\in\{1,-1\}}v_{1}^{a_{1}\oplus_{2}b_{1}}\right)\left(\frac{1}{2}\sum_{v_{2}\in\{1,-1\}}v_{2}^{a_{2}\oplus_{2}b_{2}}\right)\cdots\left(\frac{1}{2}\sum_{v_{n}\in\{1,-1\}}v_{n}^{a_{n}\oplus_{2}b_{n}}\right)
={1i​f​fai=bi⟹ai⊕bi=0​∀i∈{1,2,…​n}0​o​t​h​e​r​w​i​s​e​a​s​∃k∈{1,2​…​n}​s.t​ak⊕bk=1⟹∑vk∈{1,−1}vk=0\displaystyle=\begin{cases}1\>\>\>\>\>iff\>\>\>\>\>\>a_{i}=b_{i}\implies a_{i}\oplus b_{i}=0\>\>\forall i\in\{1,2,...n\}\\ 0\>\>\>\>otherwise\>\>\>as\>\>\exists k\in\{1,2...n\}\>\>s.t\>\>\>a_{k}\oplus b_{k}=1\implies\sum_{v_{k}\in\{1,-1\}}v_{k}=0\end{cases}

where ‘⊕2\oplus_{2}’ is a modulo 2 sum, which behaves as an XOR operation since the variables aia_{i} and bib_{i} are binary. ∎

Lemma B.2.

(Approach 2 : Use of indicator functions) Let us define an indicator function Ih→​(v→):𝕍→ℝI_{\vec{h}}(\vec{v}):\mathbb{V}\to\mathbb{R} as:

Ih→​(v→)=∏k12​(1+vkhk)={1if ​v→=h→0if ​v→≠h→\displaystyle I_{\vec{h}}(\vec{v})=\prod_{k}\frac{1}{2}\left(1+\frac{v_{k}}{h_{k}}\right)=\begin{cases}1&\text{if }\vec{v}=\vec{h}\\ 0&\text{if }\vec{v}\neq\vec{h}\end{cases} (18)

where v→,h→∈𝕍\vec{v},\vec{h}\in\mathbb{V}. The set 𝒮={Ih(i)​(v→)∣h(i)∈V}\mathcal{S}=\{I_{h^{(i)}}(\vec{v})\mid h^{(i)}\in V\} act as a basis for the function space f:𝕍→ℝf:\mathbb{V}\to\mathbb{R}.

Proof.

We establish the assertion above by using the following claims

  1. 1.

    Claim 1: The set S defined above consists of linearly independent items i.e. ∑i=02n−1ci​(Ih(i)​(v→))=0∀v→∈𝕍⇔ci=0∀i\sum_{i=0}^{2^{n}-1}c_{i}\left(I_{h^{(i)}}(\vec{v})\right)=0\quad\forall\vec{v}\in\mathbb{V}\iff c_{i}=0\quad\forall i

    Subproof.

    To demonstrate this let us recall that |S|=2n|S|=2^{n} as it contains one Ih(i)​(v→)I_{h^{(i)}}(\vec{v}) for every h(i)∈𝕍h^{(i)}\in\mathbb{V}. The condition of linear independence will have to be true for every v→∈𝕍\vec{v}\in\mathbb{V} which will actually generate a set of 2n2^{n} linear equations that will need to be solved. It is easy to show that the null space of the matrix kernel generating the set of linear equations contains only a trivial entry. For example if we investigate the veracity of the condition by substituting a specific configuration say v→=v→(k)\vec{v}=\vec{v}^{(k)}

    ∑i=02n−1\displaystyle\sum_{i=0}^{2^{n}-1} ci​(Ih(i)​(v→(k)))=0\displaystyle c_{i}\left(I_{h^{(i)}}(\vec{v}^{(k)})\right)=0 (19)
    ⟹\displaystyle\implies c0(Ih(0)(v→(k)))+c1(Ih(1)(v→(k)))+⋅⋅ck(Ih(k)(v→(k)))+⋅⋅c2n−1(Ih(2n−1)(v→(k)))=0\displaystyle c_{0}\left(I_{h^{(0)}}(\vec{v}^{(k)})\right)+c_{1}\left(I_{h^{(1)}}(\vec{v}^{(k)})\right)+\cdot\cdot c_{k}\left(I_{h^{(k)}}(\vec{v}^{(k)})\right)+\cdot\cdot c_{2^{n}-1}\left(I_{h^{(2^{n}-1)}}(\vec{v}^{(k)})\right)=0
    ⟹\displaystyle\implies ck​(Ih(k)​(v→(k)))=0\because​Ih(k)​(v→(j))=0​i​f​j≠k\displaystyle c_{k}\left(I_{h^{(k)}}(\vec{v}^{(k)})\right)=0\>\>\>\>\>\>\>\>\>\>\>\because\>\>\>I_{h^{(k)}}(\vec{v}^{(j)})=0\>\>if\>\>j\neq k
    ⟹\displaystyle\implies ck=0\because​Ih(k)​(v→(k))=1\displaystyle c_{k}=0\>\>\>\>\>\>\>\>\>\>\because\>\>\>I_{h^{(k)}}(\vec{v}^{(k)})=1

    Since no assumption is made on the nature/choice of the configuration v→(k)\vec{v}^{(k)}, this can be proven to be true for any of the 2n2^{n} configurations in set 𝕍\mathbb{V}. This means that ci=0​∀i∈{0,1,..2n−1}c_{i}=0\>\>\forall\>\>i\in\>\>\{0,1,..2^{n-1}\} which establishes forward direction of the claim. The reverse direction i.e. if ci=0​∀ic_{i}=0\>\>\forall\>\>i then ∑i=02n−1ci⋅(Ih(i)​(v→))=0\sum_{i=0}^{2^{n}-1}c_{i}\cdot\left(I_{h^{(i)}}(\vec{v})\right)=0 is trivially true. ∎

  2. 2.

    Claim 2: The set S defined above have enough degrees of freedom to span the space of functions f:𝕍→ℝf:\mathbb{V}\to\mathbb{R}

    Subproof.

    To demonstrate this we investigate a specific linear combination of the kind g⁡(v→)=∑i=02n−1ci​(Ih(i)​(v→))g(\vec{v})=\sum_{i=0}^{2^{n}-1}c_{i}\left(I_{h^{(i)}}(\vec{v})\right). Using Claim 1 , we already know that g⁡(v→)=0g(\vec{v})=0 iff ci=0​∀ic_{i}=0\>\>\forall i. This establishes the inability to express any Ih(i)​(v→)I_{h^{(i)}}(\vec{v}) in terms of other elements of the set SS above and makes the number of independently tunable coefficients in C=(c0,c1,….c2n−1)C=(c_{0},c_{1},....c^{2^{n}-1}) to 2n2^{n}, one for each of the unique entries h(i)∈𝕍h^{(i)}\in\mathbb{V} where |S|=2n|S|=2^{n}. This should already provide expressible guarantees to any f:𝕍→ℝf:\mathbb{V}\to\mathbb{R} given such a function can at most have 2n2^{n} independently tunable components for entry v→∈𝕍\vec{v}\in\mathbb{V} and be completely specified by delineating these entries. Let us now imagine that we would like to construct such a function f⁡(v→)f(\vec{v}) such that f⁡(v→(k))=g⁡(v→(k))f(\vec{v}^{(k)})=g(\vec{v}^{(k)}) for every v→(k)∈𝕍\vec{v}^{(k)}\in\mathbb{V}. In other words akin to Lagrange interpolation, g⁡(v→)g(\vec{v}) would serve as an interpolating polynomial for f⁡(v→)f(\vec{v}).

    f⁡(v→(k))≡g⁡(v→(k))\displaystyle f(\vec{v}^{(k)})\equiv g(\vec{v}^{(k)}) =\displaystyle= ∑i=02n−1ci​(Ih(i)​(v→(k)))\displaystyle\sum_{i=0}^{2^{n}-1}c_{i}\left(I_{h^{(i)}}(\vec{v}^{(k)})\right)
    =\displaystyle= ck​(Ih(k)​(v→(k)))\because​Ih(k)​(v→(j))=0​i​f​j≠k\displaystyle c_{k}\left(I_{h^{(k)}}(\vec{v}^{(k)})\right)\>\>\>\>\>\>\>\>\>\>\>\because\>\>\>I_{h^{(k)}}(\vec{v}^{(j)})=0\>\>if\>\>j\neq k
    f⁡(v→(k))\displaystyle f(\vec{v}^{(k)}) =\displaystyle= ck\because​Ih(k)​(v→(k))=1\displaystyle c_{k}\>\>\>\>\>\>\>\>\>\>\>\>\>\because\>\>\>I_{h^{(k)}}(\vec{v}^{(k)})=1 (20)

    As before since no assumption is made on the nature/choice of the configuration v→(k)\vec{v}^{(k)}, this can be proven to be true for any of the 2n2^{n} configurations in set 𝕍\mathbb{V} i.e. f⁡(v→(k))=ck​∀k∈{0,1,..2n−1}f(\vec{v}^{(k)})=c_{k}\>\>\>\>\forall k\>\>\in\{0,1,..2^{n-1}\}. It must be also be emphasized that neither f⁡(v→)f(\vec{v}) nor g⁡(v→)g(\vec{v}) is defined at any other points other than v→∈𝕍\vec{v}\in\mathbb{V} due to discreteness of their domains which makes f⁡(v→(k))=g⁡(v→(k))f(\vec{v}^{(k)})=g(\vec{v}^{(k)}) at all conceivable points. Also there is no restriction on the components f⁡(v→(k))f(\vec{v}^{(k)}) too and they can be arbitrarily set to create any function. Thus it is always possible to find a representation of an arbitrary function f⁡(v→)=∑i=02n−1f⁡(h→(i))​(Ih(i)​(v→))f(\vec{v})=\sum_{i=0}^{2^{n}-1}f(\vec{h}^{(i)})\left(I_{h^{(i)}}(\vec{v})\right) ∎

Together Claim1 and Claim2 proves the assertion stated. ∎

Lemma B.3.

For any arbitrary f:𝕍→ℝf:\mathbb{V}\to\mathbb{R} one can represent f⁡(v→)=∑a→∈{0,1}nca→​Fa→​(v→)f(\vec{v})=\sum_{\vec{a}\in\{0,1\}^{n}}c_{\vec{a}}F_{\vec{a}}(\vec{v}) where ca→∈ℝc_{\vec{a}}\in\mathbb{R}

Proof.

Given an arbitrary f:𝕍→ℝf:\mathbb{V}\to\mathbb{R} we can do the following:

f⁡(v→)\displaystyle f(\vec{v}) =\displaystyle= ∑i=02n−1f⁡(h→(i))​(Ih(i)​(v→))\because​L​e​m​m​a​B.2\displaystyle\sum_{i=0}^{2^{n}-1}f(\vec{h}^{(i)})\left(I_{h^{(i)}}(\vec{v})\right)\>\>\>\>\>\>\>\because Lemma\>\>\ref{lem:indicator_formalism_LI}
=\displaystyle= ∑i=02n−1f⁡(h→(i))​∏kn12​(1+vkhk(i))\displaystyle\sum_{i=0}^{2^{n}-1}f(\vec{h}^{(i)})\prod_{k}^{n}\frac{1}{2}\left(1+\frac{v_{k}}{h_{k}^{(i)}}\right)
=\displaystyle= ∑i=02n−1f⁡(h→(i))​12n​∑a→∈{0,1}n∏kn(vkhk(i))ak∀k​ak∈{0,1},a→=(a0,a1​…​an)\displaystyle\sum_{i=0}^{2^{n}-1}f(\vec{h}^{(i)})\frac{1}{2^{n}}\sum_{\vec{a}\in\{0,1\}^{n}}\prod_{k}^{n}\left(\frac{v_{k}}{h_{k}^{(i)}}\right)^{a_{k}}\>\>\>\>\>\forall k\>\>a_{k}\in\{0,1\},\>\>\vec{a}=(a_{0},a_{1}...a_{n})
=\displaystyle= ∑i=02n−1f⁡(h→(i))​12n​∑a→∈{0,1}n∏knvkak​∏kn(hk(i))−ak\because​hk(i)∈{1,−1}\displaystyle\sum_{i=0}^{2^{n}-1}f(\vec{h}^{(i)})\frac{1}{2^{n}}\sum_{\vec{a}\in\{0,1\}^{n}}\prod_{k}^{n}v_{k}^{a_{k}}\prod_{k}^{n}\left(h_{k}^{(i)}\right)^{-a_{k}}\>\>\>\>\>\because\>\>h_{k}^{(i)}\>\in\>\{1,-1\}
=\displaystyle= ∑a→∈{0,1}n(12n​∑i=02n−1f⁡(h→(i))​∏kn(hk(i))−ak)⏟=ca→∈ℝ​\because​f​(h→(i))∈ℝ​∏knvkak\displaystyle\sum_{\vec{a}\in\{0,1\}^{n}}\underbrace{\left(\frac{1}{2^{n}}\sum_{i=0}^{2^{n}-1}f(\vec{h}^{(i)})\prod_{k}^{n}\left(h_{k}^{(i)}\right)^{-a_{k}}\right)}_{=c_{\vec{a}}\>\in\>\>\mathbb{R}\>\>\>\>\because\>\>\>f(\vec{h}^{(i)})\>\>\in\>\>\mathbb{R}}\prod_{k}^{n}v_{k}^{a_{k}}
=\displaystyle= ∑a→∈{0,1}nca→​∏knvkak\displaystyle\sum_{\vec{a}\in\{0,1\}^{n}}c_{\vec{a}}\prod_{k}^{n}v_{k}^{a_{k}}
=\displaystyle= ∑a→∈{0,1}nca→Fa→(v→)v→=(v1,v2,..vn),Fa→(v→)=∏iviai\displaystyle\sum_{\vec{a}\in\{0,1\}^{n}}c_{\vec{a}}F_{\vec{a}}(\vec{v})\>\>\>\>\>\>\>\>\vec{v}=(v_{1},v_{2},..v_{n}),\>\>F_{\vec{a}}(\vec{v})=\prod_{i}v_{i}^{a_{i}}

Alternatively we could also use the assertion of Lemma  B.1, to claim that the set χ\chi forms a linearly independent set. There are 2n2^{n} monomials Fa→​(v→)F_{\vec{a}}(\vec{v}) given each is characterized by a distinct a→∈{0,1}n\vec{a}\in\{0,1\}^{n} so |χ|=2n|\chi|=2^{n}. Since any arbitrary function f:𝕍→ℝf:\mathbb{V}\to\mathbb{R} would possess 2n2^{n} independent components, the set of monomials χ\chi can span the space as a basis. ∎

Lemma B.4.

Any arbitrary probability distribution P:𝕍→[0,1]P:\mathbb{V}\to[0,1] defined over a finite support of bit-strings v→∈𝕍\vec{v}\in\mathbb{V} can be written in the form

P⁡(v→)=e∑a→∈{0,1}n,a→≠0→Ca→​Fa→​(v→)∑v→e∑a→∈{0,1}n,a→≠0→Ca→​Fa→​(v→)\displaystyle P(\vec{v})=\frac{e^{\sum_{\vec{a}\in\{0,1\}^{n},\vec{a}\neq\vec{0}}C_{\vec{a}}F_{\vec{a}}(\vec{v})}}{\sum_{\vec{v}}e^{\sum_{\vec{a}\in\{0,1\}^{n},\vec{a}\neq\vec{0}}C_{\vec{a}}F_{\vec{a}}(\vec{v})}} (21)

where Fa→(v→)=v1a1v2a2⋯vnan=∏iviaia→=(a1,a2….an)withai∈{0,1}F_{\vec{a}}(\vec{v})=v_{1}^{a_{1}}v_{2}^{a_{2}}\cdots v_{n}^{a_{n}}=\prod_{i}v_{i}^{a_{i}}\>\>\>\vec{a}=(a_{1},a_{2}....a_{n})\>\>with\>\>a_{i}\in\{0,1\} and Ca→∈ℝC_{\vec{a}}\in\mathbb{R}.

Proof.

Let us define a function f⁡(v→)=log⁡(P⁡(v→))f(\vec{v})=\log(P(\vec{v})) where P⁡(v→)P(\vec{v}) is the discrete probability distribution of interest. Given P:𝕍→[0,1]P:\mathbb{V}\to[0,1], we then have log⁡(P):𝕍→[−∞,0]\log(P):\mathbb{V}\to[-\infty,0]. We can make the domain of log⁡(P)∈ℝ\log(P)\in\mathbb{R} if for every v(k)∈𝕍v^{(k)}\in\mathbb{V} for which P⁡(v→(k))=0P(\vec{v}^{(k)})=0, we can replace P⁡(v→(k))≈ϵP(\vec{v}^{(k)})\approx\epsilon where ϵ→0+\epsilon\to 0_{+}. This will ensure log(P):𝕍→(−∞,0]⊂ℝ\log(P):\mathbb{V}\to(-\infty,0]\subset\mathbb{R} for which the assertions of the above lemmas hold true. With this substitution one can do the following

f⁡(v→)\displaystyle f(\vec{v}) =\displaystyle= log⁡(P⁡(v→))\displaystyle\log(P(\vec{v}))
=\displaystyle= ∑a→∈{0,1}nCa→​Fa→​(v→)\because​L​e​m​m​a​B.3\displaystyle\sum_{\vec{a}\in\{0,1\}^{n}}C_{\vec{a}}F_{\vec{a}}(\vec{v})\>\>\>\>\>\>\because\>\>Lemma\>\>\ref{lem:ind_basis_to_mono}
=\displaystyle= C0+∑a→∈{0,1}n,a→≠0→Ca→​Fa→​(v→)\displaystyle C_{0}+\sum_{\vec{a}\in\{0,1\}^{n},\vec{a}\neq\vec{0}}C_{\vec{a}}F_{\vec{a}}(\vec{v})
P⁡(v→)\displaystyle P(\vec{v}) =\displaystyle= eC0​e∑a→∈{0,1}n,a→≠0→Ca→​Fa→​(v→)\displaystyle e^{C_{0}}e^{\sum_{\vec{a}\in\{0,1\}^{n},\vec{a}\neq\vec{0}}C_{\vec{a}}F_{\vec{a}}(\vec{v})} (22)

From Eq.22 it is clear that P⁡(v→)=e∑a→∈{0,1}n,a→≠0→Ca→​Fa→​(v→)∑v→e∑a→∈{0,1}n,a→≠0→Ca→​Fa→​(v→)P(\vec{v})=\frac{e^{\sum_{\vec{a}\in\{0,1\}^{n},\vec{a}\neq\vec{0}}C_{\vec{a}}F_{\vec{a}}(\vec{v})}}{\sum_{\vec{v}}e^{\sum_{\vec{a}\in\{0,1\}^{n},\vec{a}\neq\vec{0}}C_{\vec{a}}F_{\vec{a}}(\vec{v})}} where eC0=1∑v→e∑a→∈{0,1}n,a→≠0→Ca→​Fa→​(v→)e^{C_{0}}=\frac{1}{\sum_{\vec{v}}e^{\sum_{\vec{a}\in\{0,1\}^{n},\vec{a}\neq\vec{0}}C_{\vec{a}}F_{\vec{a}}(\vec{v})}} by normalization. ∎

Using Lemma B.4, Lemma B.3, Claim 2 we are now in the position to prove the Theorem II.1 in main manuscript which is reproduced here for completeness and continuity

Theorem B.1.

Given 𝕍={v→|v→∈{−1,1}n}\mathbb{V}=\{\vec{v}|\vec{v}\in\{-1,1\}^{n}\} where n∈ℤ+n\in\mathbb{Z}_{+} and an arbitrary discrete probability distribution P:𝕍→[0,1]P:\mathbb{V}\to[0,1], then the following statement is true

  1. 1.

    It is always possible to find a representation of P⁡(v→)P(\vec{v}) as

    P⁡(v→)\displaystyle P(\vec{v}) =\displaystyle= 𝒩​κ​(v→)​e∑a→∈{0,1}n,H⁡(a→)≤kCa→​Fa→​(v→)∑v→e∑a→∈{0,1}n,H⁡(a→)≤kCa→​Fa→​(v→)\displaystyle\mathcal{N}\kappa(\vec{v})\frac{e^{\sum_{\vec{a}\in\{0,1\}^{n},H(\vec{a})\leq k}C_{\vec{a}}F_{\vec{a}}(\vec{v})}}{\sum_{\vec{v}}e^{\sum_{\vec{a}\in\{0,1\}^{n},H(\vec{a})\leq k}C_{\vec{a}}F_{\vec{a}}(\vec{v})}} (23)
    =\displaystyle= 𝒩​κ​(v→)​ϕ​(v→)\displaystyle\mathcal{N}\kappa(\vec{v})\phi(\vec{v})

    where Fa→(v→)=∏iviai,a→=(a1,a2….an)∈{0,1}n,v→=(v1,v2,…vn)∈𝕍F_{\vec{a}}(\vec{v})=\prod_{i}v_{i}^{a_{i}}\>\>\>,\vec{a}=(a_{1},a_{2}....a_{n})\in\{0,1\}^{n},\>\>\>\>\vec{v}=(v_{1},v_{2},...v_{n})\>\>\in\mathbb{V}, Ca→∈ℝ\>\>\>C_{\vec{a}}\in\mathbb{R}, and H⁡(a→)=∑inaiH(\vec{a})=\sum_{i}^{n}a_{i} is the Hamming weight of a→\vec{a}. We have defined ϕ⁡(v→)=e∑a→∈{0,1}n,H⁡(a→)≤kCa→​Fa→​(v→)∑v→e∑a→∈{0,1}n,H⁡(a→)≤kCa→​Fa→​(v→)\phi(\vec{v})=\frac{e^{\sum_{\vec{a}\in\{0,1\}^{n},H(\vec{a})\leq k}C_{\vec{a}}F_{\vec{a}}(\vec{v})}}{\sum_{\vec{v}}e^{\sum_{\vec{a}\in\{0,1\}^{n},H(\vec{a})\leq k}C_{\vec{a}}F_{\vec{a}}(\vec{v})}} as another discrete distribution ϕ:𝕍→[0,1]\phi:\mathbb{V}\to[0,1] which will be the backbone of a secondary surrogate network. Also 𝒩≠f⁡(v→)≥0\mathcal{N}\neq f(\vec{v})\geq 0 and k∈ℤ+k\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}, is a user-defined preset non-negative integer. kk controls the degree of the polynomial chosen for expressing ϕ⁡(v→)\phi(\vec{v}).

  2. 2.

    κ⁡(v→)\kappa(\vec{v}) is a configuration dependant non-negative prefactor. In the most generic case, ∃\exists M∈ℝ≥0M\in\mathbb{R}\geq 0 such that |log⁡(κ⁡(v→))||\log(\kappa(\vec{v}))| is upper bounded as

    |log⁡(κ⁡(v→))|≤M⁡(2n−∑j=0kCjn)\displaystyle|\log(\kappa(\vec{v}))|\leq M\left(2^{n}-\sum_{j=0}^{k}\ {}^{n}C_{j}\right) (24)
Proof.

We establish each of the assertions as follows:

  1. 1.

    Statement 1: P⁡(v→)=𝒩​κ​(v→)​e∑a→∈{0,1}n,H⁡(a→)≤kCa→​Fa→​(v→)∑v→e∑a→∈{0,1}n,H⁡(a→)≤kCa→​Fa→​(v→)=𝒩​κ​(v→)​ϕ​(v→)P(\vec{v})=\mathcal{N}\kappa(\vec{v})\frac{e^{\sum_{\vec{a}\in\{0,1\}^{n},H(\vec{a})\leq k}C_{\vec{a}}F_{\vec{a}}(\vec{v})}}{\sum_{\vec{v}}e^{\sum_{\vec{a}\in\{0,1\}^{n},H(\vec{a})\leq k}C_{\vec{a}}F_{\vec{a}}(\vec{v})}}=\mathcal{N}\kappa(\vec{v})\phi(\vec{v})

    Subproof.

    We can prove this assertion the following way

Appendix C Alteration in Variance of the Sampled estimate of the local energy due to parameterization of κ⁡(v→)\kappa(\vec{v})

We would like to prove in this section that certain choices/parameterization of κ⁡(v→)\kappa(\vec{v}) introduced in previous section can lead to reduction in variance of the sampled estimate of a random variable. However, before we delve into that we first show that the mean of the random variable using samples generated from the surrogate distribution of ϕ⁡(v→)\phi(\vec{v}) is an unbiased estimator of the target sample estimate computed using the original distribution P⁡(v→)=ρvv​(X→)P(\vec{v})=\rho^{v}_{v}(\vec{X}) (see main text). In other words, mean of a random variable of interest(El​o​c​(v)E_{loc}(v)) over the distribution ρvv\rho^{v}_{v} is equivalent to the mean of El​o​c​(v)​κ​(v)E_{loc}(v)\kappa(v) over the distribution ϕ⁡(v)\phi(v). We do this by using the following lemma

Lemma C.1.

Means obtained from ρvv\rho_{v}^{v} and ϕ⁡(v)\phi(v): The mean obtained by averaging El​o​c​(v)E_{loc}(v) over probability distribution ρvv\rho_{v}^{v} is the same as the mean of El​o​c​(v)​κ​(v)E_{loc}(v)\kappa(v) over probability distribution ϕ⁡(v)\phi(v).

⟨H⟩=⟨El​o​c​(v)⟩ρvv=⟨El​o​c​(v)​κ​(v)⟩ϕ⁡(v){\langle H\rangle=\langle E_{loc}(v)\rangle_{\rho_{v}^{v}}=\langle E_{loc}(v)\kappa(v)\rangle_{\phi(v)}}
Proof.
⟨H⟩\displaystyle\langle H\rangle =T​r​(ρ​H)\displaystyle=Tr(\rho H)
=∑vρvv​(∑v′ρv′v​Hvv′ρvv)\displaystyle=\sum_{v}\rho_{v}^{v}\Big(\frac{\sum_{v^{\prime}}\rho_{v^{\prime}}^{v}H_{v}^{v^{\prime}}}{\rho_{v}^{v}}\Big)
=∑vρvv​El​o​c​(v)=⟨El​o​c​(v)⟩ρvv\displaystyle=\sum_{v}\rho_{v}^{v}E_{loc}(v)=\langle E_{loc}(v)\rangle_{\rho_{v}^{v}} (26)
⟨El​o​c​(v)​κ​(v)⟩ϕ⁡(v)\displaystyle\langle E_{loc}(v)\kappa(v)\rangle_{\phi(v)}
=∑vEl​o​c​(v)​κ​(v)​ϕ​(v)\displaystyle=\sum_{v}E_{loc}(v)\kappa(v)\phi(v)
=∑vEl​o​c​(v)​ρvv\displaystyle=\sum_{v}E_{loc}(v)\rho_{v}^{v}
=⟨El​o​c​(v)⟩ρvv\displaystyle=\langle E_{loc}(v)\rangle_{\rho_{v}^{v}} (27)

Thus from 26 and 27,

⟨H⟩=⟨El​o​c​(v)⟩ρvv=⟨El​o​c​(v)​κ​(v)⟩ϕ⁡(v)\displaystyle\boxed{\langle H\rangle=\langle E_{loc}(v)\rangle_{\rho_{v}^{v}}=\langle E_{loc}(v)\kappa(v)\rangle_{\phi(v)}} (28)

∎

Thus we see we have access to two distributions ρvv\rho_{v}^{v} and ϕ⁡(v)\phi(v). If we sample vv from either and compute the mean of two different random variables, i.e., El​o​c​(v)E_{loc}(v) for ρvv\rho_{v}^{v} and El​o​c​(v)​κ​(v)E_{loc}(v)\kappa(v) for ϕ⁡(v)\phi(v), then the population mean of the two would be equal. The mean of either of these two random variables can act as a proxy of the other.

Now we would like to prove the main theorem in this Section

Theorem C.1.

Variances obtained from ρvv\rho_{v}^{v} and ϕ⁡(v)\phi(v): For a specific form of κ⁡(v)=1λ​|El​o​c​(v)|α\kappa(v)=\frac{1}{\lambda|E_{loc}(v)|^{\alpha}}, the difference between the variance of the sampled random variable El​o​c​(v)E_{loc}(v) over ρvv\rho_{v}^{v} and the variance of El​o​c​(v)​κ​(v)E_{loc}(v)\kappa(v) over ϕ⁡(v)\phi(v) is given by,

σEl​o​c​(v)2−σEl​o​c​(v)​κ​(v)2=Cov​(|El​o​c​(v)|2−α,|El​o​c​(v)|α)\sigma_{E_{loc}(v)}^{2}-\sigma_{E_{loc}(v)\kappa(v)}^{2}=\text{Cov}\left(|E_{loc}(v)|^{2-\alpha},|E_{loc}(v)|^{\alpha}\right)
Proof.
σEl​o​c​(v)2\displaystyle\sigma_{E_{loc}(v)}^{2} =∑vEl​o​c2​(v)​ρvv−⟨El​o​c​(v)⟩ρvv2\displaystyle=\sum_{v}E^{2}_{loc}(v)\rho_{v}^{v}-\langle E_{loc}(v)\rangle_{\rho_{v}^{v}}^{2}
σEl​o​c​(v)​κ​(v)2\displaystyle\sigma_{E_{loc}(v)\kappa(v)}^{2} =∑vEl​o​c​(v)​κ​(v)2​ϕ​(v)−⟨El​o​c​(v)​κ​(v)⟩ϕ⁡(v)2\displaystyle=\sum_{v}E_{loc}(v)\kappa(v)^{2}\phi(v)-\langle E_{loc}(v)\kappa(v)\rangle_{\phi(v)}^{2}

This can tell us how far are each individual estimate of random variable (El​o​c​(v)E_{loc}(v) for ρvv\rho_{v}^{v} but El​o​c​(v)​κ​(v)E_{loc}(v)\kappa(v) for ϕ⁡(v)\phi(v)) differ from their respective means (which by construction, see 28, are equivalent). Also, in the respective Chebyshev inequality, it is the variance of the respective means that sits and it is not the same random variable.

P⁡(|El​o​c​(v)​κ​(v)−⟨El​o​c​(v)​κ​(v)⟩ϕ⁡(v)|≥ϵ)≤Var​(El​o​c​(v)​κ​(v))Ns​ϵ2P(|E_{loc}(v)\kappa(v)-\langle E_{loc}(v)\kappa(v)\rangle_{\phi(v)}|\geq\epsilon)\leq\frac{\text{Var}(E_{loc}(v)\kappa(v))}{N_{s}\,\epsilon^{2}}
P⁡(|El​o​c​(v)−⟨El​o​c​(v)⟩ρvv|≥ϵ)≤Var​(El​o​c​(v))Ns​ϵ2P(|E_{loc}(v)-\langle E_{loc}(v)\rangle_{\rho_{v}^{v}}|\geq\epsilon)\leq\frac{\text{Var}(E_{loc}(v))}{N_{s}\,\epsilon^{2}}

We need to see for the same NsN_{s} if the variances Var​(El​o​c​(v)​κ​(v)),Var​(El​o​c​(v))\text{Var}(E_{loc}(v)\kappa(v)),\text{Var}(E_{loc}(v)) are equivalent or not?

Thus, Var​(El​o​c​(v))ρvv−Var​(El​o​c​(v)​κ​(v))ϕ⁡(v)\displaystyle\text{Var}(E_{loc}(v))_{\rho_{v}^{v}}-\text{Var}(E_{loc}(v)\kappa(v))_{\phi(v)}
=σEl​o​c​(v)2−σEl​o​c​(v)​κ​(v)2\displaystyle=\sigma^{2}_{E_{loc}(v)}-\sigma_{E_{loc}(v)\kappa(v)}^{2}
=∑vEl​o​c2​(v)​ρvv−∑v(El​o​c​(v)​κ​(v))2​ϕ​(v)+⟨El​o​c​(v)​κ​(v)⟩ϕ⁡(v)2−⟨El​o​c​(v)⟩ρvv2\displaystyle=\sum_{v}E^{2}_{loc}(v)\rho_{v}^{v}-\sum_{v}(E_{loc}(v)\kappa(v))^{2}\phi(v)+\langle E_{loc}(v)\kappa(v)\rangle_{\phi(v)}^{2}-\langle E_{loc}(v)\rangle_{\rho_{v}^{v}}^{2}
=∑vEl​o​c2​(v)​ρvv−∑v(El​o​c​(v)​κ​(v))2​ϕ​(v)\displaystyle=\sum_{v}E^{2}_{loc}(v)\rho_{v}^{v}-\sum_{v}(E_{loc}(v)\kappa(v))^{2}\phi(v)
=∑vEl​o​c2​(v)​ρvv−∑vEl​o​c2​(v)​κ2​(v)​ϕ​(v)\displaystyle=\sum_{v}E^{2}_{loc}(v)\rho_{v}^{v}-\sum_{v}E^{2}_{loc}(v)\kappa^{2}(v)\phi(v)
=∑vEl​o​c2​(v)​ρvv−∑vEl​o​c2​(v)​(ρvv)2ϕ⁡(v)\displaystyle=\sum_{v}E^{2}_{loc}(v)\rho_{v}^{v}-\sum_{v}\frac{E^{2}_{loc}(v)\left(\rho_{v}^{v}\right)^{2}}{\phi(v)}
=∑vEl​o​c2​(v)​ρvv​(1−ρvvϕ⁡(v))\displaystyle=\sum_{v}E^{2}_{loc}(v)\rho_{v}^{v}\left(1-\frac{\rho_{v}^{v}}{\phi(v)}\right)

Now if we assume  κ⁡(v)=1λ​|El​o​c​(v)|α⟹ϕ⁡(v)=λ​|El​o​c​(v)|α​ρvv\boxed{\kappa(v)=\frac{1}{\lambda|E_{loc}(v)|^{\alpha}}\implies\phi(v)=\lambda|E_{loc}(v)|^{\alpha}\rho_{v}^{v}}

then λ=∑vϕ⁡(v)∑v|El​o​c​(v)|α​ρvv=1∑v|El​o​c​(v)|α​ρvv\displaystyle\quad\lambda=\frac{\sum_{v}\phi(v)}{\sum_{v}|E_{loc}(v)|^{\alpha}\rho_{v}^{v}}=\frac{1}{\sum_{v}|E_{loc}(v)|^{\alpha}\rho_{v}^{v}}
or ϕ⁡(v)=|El​o​c​(v)|α​ρvv∑v′|El​o​c​(v′)|α​ρv′v′\displaystyle\quad\phi(v)=\frac{|E_{loc}(v)|^{\alpha}\rho_{v}^{v}}{\sum_{v^{\prime}}|E_{loc}(v^{\prime})|^{\alpha}\rho_{v^{\prime}}^{v^{\prime}}}
or ρvvϕ⁡(v)=∑v′|El​o​c​(v′)|α​ρv′v′|El​o​c​(v)|α\displaystyle\quad\frac{\rho_{v}^{v}}{\phi(v)}=\frac{\sum_{v^{\prime}}|E_{loc}(v^{\prime})|^{\alpha}\rho_{v^{\prime}}^{v^{\prime}}}{|E_{loc}(v)|^{\alpha}}

In other words, we have

σEl​o​c​(v)2−σEl​o​c​(v)​κ​(v)2\displaystyle\sigma_{E_{loc}(v)}^{2}-\sigma_{E_{loc}(v)\kappa(v)}^{2}
=∑vEl​o​c2​(v)​ρvv​(1−∑v′|El​o​c​(v′)|α​ρv′v′|El​o​c​(v)|α)\displaystyle=\sum_{v}E^{2}_{loc}(v)\rho_{v}^{v}\left(1-\frac{\sum_{v^{\prime}}|E_{loc}(v^{\prime})|^{\alpha}\rho_{v^{\prime}}^{v^{\prime}}}{|E_{loc}(v)|^{\alpha}}\right)
=∑vEl​o​c2​(v)​ρvv​(1−⟨|El​o​c​(v)|α⟩ρvv|El​o​c​(v)|α)\displaystyle=\sum_{v}E^{2}_{loc}(v)\rho_{v}^{v}\left(1-\frac{\langle|E_{loc}(v)|^{\alpha}\rangle_{\rho_{v}^{v}}}{|E_{loc}(v)|^{\alpha}}\right) (29)
=∑vEl​o​c2​(v)​ρvv−(∑vEl​o​c2​(v)​ρvv|El​o​c​(v)|α)​⟨|El​o​c​(v)|α⟩ρvv\displaystyle=\sum_{v}E^{2}_{loc}(v)\rho_{v}^{v}-\left(\sum_{v}\frac{E^{2}_{loc}(v)\rho_{v}^{v}}{|E_{loc}(v)|^{\alpha}}\right)\left\langle|E_{loc}(v)|^{\alpha}\right\rangle_{\rho_{v}^{v}} (30)

=Cov​(|El​o​c​(v)|2−α,|El​o​c​(v)|α)\displaystyle=\text{Cov}\left(|E_{loc}(v)|^{2-\alpha},|E_{loc}(v)|^{\alpha}\right) (32)

Or

σEl​o​c​(v)2−σEl​o​c​(v)​κ​(v)2=Cov​(|El​o​c​(v)|2−α,|El​o​c​(v)|α)\boxed{\sigma_{E_{loc}(v)}^{2}-\sigma_{E_{loc}(v)\kappa(v)}^{2}=\text{Cov}\left(|E_{loc}(v)|^{2-\alpha},|E_{loc}(v)|^{\alpha}\right)} (33)

=𝔼⁡[(Z−⟨Z⟩)​(g⁡(Z)+g⁡(⟨Z⟩)−g⁡(Z)−⟨g⁡(Z)⟩)]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[(Z-\langle Z\rangle)(g(Z)+g(\langle Z\rangle)-g(Z)-\langle g(Z)\rangle)\right]

=𝔼⁡[(Z−⟨Z⟩)​(g⁡(Z)−g⁡(⟨Z⟩))]+𝔼⁡[(Z−⟨Z⟩)​(g⁡(⟨Z⟩)−⟨g⁡(Z)⟩)]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[(Z-\langle Z\rangle)(g(Z)-g(\langle Z\rangle))]+\mathbb{E}[(Z-\langle Z\rangle)(g(\langle Z\rangle)-\langle g(Z)\rangle)]

Appendix D Data driven construction of the surrogate probability distribution

In the previous sections, we have shown that any probability distribution can be written in terms of an exponential of an arbitrary-degree polynomial function of the spin configuration (see Theorem II.1 in main manuscript or Theorem B.1 in Section S2). So far we have proven that it is always possible to represent an arbitrary probability distribution P⁡(v→):𝕍→[0,1]P(\vec{v}):\mathbb{V}\to[0,1] as 𝒩​κ​(v→)​ϕ​(v→)\mathcal{N}\kappa(\vec{v})\phi(\vec{v}) where ϕ⁡(v→)\phi(\vec{v}) is the distribution of the surrogate network defined as

ϕ(v→,X→)∝exp(−β∑ili(X→)vi+∑i​jJi​j(X→)vivj+⋯)\phi({\vec{v}},\vec{X})\propto exp\left(-\beta\sum_{i}l_{i}(\vec{X})v_{i}+\sum_{ij}J_{ij}(\vec{X})v_{i}v_{j}+\cdots\right)

Here li∈l→​(X→)l_{i}\in\vec{l}(\vec{X}) denotes the on-site field at each spin of the surrogate network and Ji​j​(X→)∈J→​(X→)J_{ij}(\vec{X})\in\vec{J}(\vec{X}) denotes the mutual coupling between a pair of spins of the surrogate. The kernel function κ⁡(v→)\kappa(\vec{v}) accounts for additional flexibility in the construction when the surrogate distribution is truncated to a finite degree kk. In this section we provide a concrete data-driven recipe to construct the same. Here we choose P⁡(v→)=ρvvP(\vec{v})=\rho_{v}^{v} where ρvv\rho_{v}^{v} is the probability distribution associated with graph G1G_{1} in main text. The surrogate so defined (see graph G2G_{2} in main text) has been truncated to second-degree i.e. k=2k=2. Even though the algorithm we describe below works for any value of kk, however, it should be noted that implementing a polynomial of degree kk requires kk-qubit gates in a quantum circuit, and hence a large kk can increase the complexity of the circuit. Therefore, one would prefer to work with low-degree polynomials for practical implementation which motivates the choice for k=2k=2. At the end of this protocol we shall have a decomposition of the following kind

ρvv​(v,X→,β)=ϕ⁡(v,X→)​κ​(v,X→,β)+ϵ⁡(v)\rho_{v}^{v}(v,\vec{X},\beta)=\phi(v,\vec{X})\kappa(v,\vec{X},\beta)\;+\epsilon(v)

where ϵ⁡(v→)\epsilon(\vec{v}) is the fitting error associated with the approximation ρvv≈ϕ⁡(v)​κ​(v)\rho_{v}^{v}\approx\phi(v)\kappa(v).

D.1 Sampling configurations for fitting

To ensure that the surrogate distribution closely approximates the actual distribution, we aim to fit the parameters of the polynomial function through a non-linear fitting process. Ideally, we would use all possible configurations to fit these parameters. However, this approach would be computationally prohibitive and moot the advantage offered by our algorithm. Therefore, we strategically select a sample of configurations to perform the fitting. The selected configurations include:

  • •

    The configurations with largest ρvv\rho_{v}^{v} value: These configurations are important because they are the most probable and thus contribute significantly to the overall distribution. We can find these configurations efficiently using the algorithm outlined below. Section D.2 Selecting these ensures that the model accurately represents the high-probability regions of the distribution.

  • •

    Random configurations, which represent the bulk of the less probable configurations. Incorporating these ensures the model generalizes well and prevents overfitting to the most probable configurations alone.

Focusing on the most probable configurations is crucial because they dominate the sampling process; these configurations have the highest ρvv\rho_{v}^{v} values and will appear most frequently during sampling. When fitting the surrogate distribution ϕ⁡(v)\phi(v), we need to ensure it performs well for these configurations since they represent the most critical part of the probability landscape. However, there is a risk associated with only using the best configurations: overfitting. If the model fits exclusively to high-probability configurations, it may perform poorly on low-probability ones. In extreme cases, this could cause the model to predict low-probability configurations so inaccurately that they interfere with high-probability predictions, compromising the overall accuracy. [See Fig 6] This is why we include random configurations in the sample. These configurations, though less probable, help to ensure that the surrogate distribution generalizes well across the entire probability space. They prevent the model from overfitting to the high-probability regions and ensure that ϕ⁡(v)\phi(v) adequately represents both high- and low-probability configurations. By constructing the surrogate network with this balanced set of configurations—both the most probable and a representative sample of lower-probability ones—we create a robust model that maintains accuracy across the full distribution without being biased toward a narrow set of configurations. We keep the split between the best configuration and random configuration as a hyperparameter. In this work, we maintain a ratio of 25% best configurations and 75% random configurations. The total number of samples is kept below O⁡(n2)O(n^{2}).

D.2 Algorithm for finding q-largest configurations

Given a probability distribution ρvv\rho_{v}^{v} which has its support over O⁡(2n)O(2^{n}) spin configurations as v→∈𝕍\vec{v}\in\mathbb{V}. We need to find qq-spin configurations that maximize ρvv\rho_{v}^{v} which from the main text is defined as: ρvv=exp(−2β∑i=1nRe(ai)vi)∏j=1m|cosh(bj+∑i=1nwi​jvi)|2\rho_{v}^{v}=\text{exp}\Big(-2\beta\sum_{i=1}^{n}Re(a_{i})v_{i}\Big)\prod_{j=1}^{m}|\cosh(b_{j}+\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_{ij}v_{i})|^{2} We exploit the structure of the probability distribution to find the qq-largest configurations. Note that the first exponential term is maximized for a configuration {vi}(0)={−sgn​(ai)}\{v_{i}\}^{(0)}=\{-\text{sgn}(a_{i})\} for i=1,…,ni=1,\dots,n. Individual cosh terms are maximized when {vi}(j)=sgn​(Re​(wi​j))\{v_{i}\}^{(j)}=\text{sgn}(\text{Re}(w_{ij})) or {vi}(m+j)=−sgn​(Re​(wi​j))\{v_{i}\}^{(m+j)}=-\text{sgn}(\text{Re}(w_{ij})) for j=1,…,mj=1,\dots,m. Starting from an initial set of 2m+1 candidates, we run an iterative algorithm that perturbs these configurations to identify the approximate qq-largest configurations.

Algorithm Steps

  1. 1.

    Initialize a list config to store the candidate spin configurations and another list result to store the spin configuration with the largest ρvv\rho_{v}^{v}.

  2. 2.

    Choose {-sgn(Re(a)), sgn(Re(wjw_{j})), and -sgn(Re(wjw_{j}))} as the first (2m+1) contenders to the largest spin configurations and store them in config. These seeds are chosen because they individually maximize different terms in ρvv\rho_{v}^{v}.

  3. 3.

    Compute ρvv\rho_{v}^{v} (upto normalization) for each (2m+1) configuration, sort them in descending order of their ρvv\rho_{v}^{v}, and remove any duplicates.

  4. 4.

    Run q iterations:

    1. (a)

      Select a configuration viv_{i} ∈\in config with the largest ρvv\rho_{v}^{v} and store it in result. Remove it from config.

    2. (b)

      Perform single-site perturbations on viv_{i}, flipping each spin to generate nn new candidate configurations {vij}j=1n\{v_{i}^{j}\}_{j=1}^{n}.

    3. (c)

      For each new configuration vijv_{i}^{j} not already in config, compute ρvv​(vij)\rho_{v}^{v}(v_{i}^{j}) and merge it into config based on its ρvv​(vij)\rho_{v}^{v}(v_{i}^{j}) values.

    4. (d)

      Trim config to maintain only the top q candidates by discarding configurations with small ρvv​(vij)\rho_{v}^{v}(v_{i}^{j}) values.

  5. 5.

    Return result - the approximate q-best configurations.

Time Complexity: The algorithm runs in O⁡(q​n)O(qn). At each iteration, we generate O⁡(n)O(n) new configurations and insert each into a sorted list. Depending on the choice of data structure, the insertion operation can take O⁡(log⁡(q))O(\log(q)) time for an array or can be done in O⁡(1)O(1) time by having a heap implementation. The nature of the algorithm is heuristic and works well with high probability for general parameter sets we dealt with so far. However, it might be possible to curate special instances where it might fail to obtain the best k configurations .

D.3 Final Fitting Algorithm

We achieve the best fit using a two-fold optimization protocol. First, we fit the logarithm of the ρvv\rho_{v}^{v} distribution to a polynomial model through a weighted least-squares (LSQ) fitting procedure. Then, we refine the results using non-linear optimization techniques, such as the Broyden–Fletcher–Goldfarb–Shanno (BFGS) algorithm. This two-step approach is necessary because the optimization landscape is highly non-convex, making the results of non-linear optimization highly sensitive to the initial parameter values. The LSQ fitting step provides a robust starting point by converging to an optimal solution with high reliability. This initial solution is then used as input for the non-linear optimization step, which fine-tunes the parameters to achieve a more accurate fit. This meticulous process is crucial because the fitting procedure plays an essential role in constructing the surrogate network. Ensuring that this mapping is as precise as possible is fundamental to the success of the entire framework.

Polynomial fitting: We transform the above non-linear fitting problem into a polynomial fitting problem by taking a logarithm of both sides.

log​ρvv​(v,X→)≈c0+∑ili​(X→)​vi+∑i,jJi​j​(X→)​vi​vj+⋯\text{log}\rho_{v}^{v}(v,\vec{X})\approx c_{0}+\sum_{i}l_{i}(\vec{X})v_{i}+\sum_{i,j}J_{ij}(\vec{X})v_{i}v_{j}+\cdots

The polynomial to be obtained by fitting has a constant term c0c_{0}, a linear term involving viv_{i}, with coefficients li​(X→)l_{i}(\vec{X}), and quadratic terms involving vi​vjv_{i}v_{j}, with coefficients Ji​j​(X→)J_{ij}(\vec{X}). Note that we restrict our discussion to polynomials with up to quadratic terms, but the method below is general for any order of polynomials.

We aim to find the optimal values for c0c_{0}, lil_{i}, and Ji​jJ_{ij} from samples ({vi}\{v^{i}\}) drawn from the distribution ρvv​(v)\rho_{v}^{v}(v) as mentioned in Section D.2. However, we want to avoid having small values of ρvv​(v)\rho_{v}^{v}(v) (which leads to highly negative log values) dominate the fitting process. Therefore, we perform a weighted fit, where the weights are proportional to ρvv​(v)\rho_{v}^{v}(v). This gives more influence to higher values of ρvv​(v)\rho_{v}^{v}(v) during the fitting process. The fitting process solves a weighted least squares (lsq) problem to find the coefficients c0c_{0}, lil_{i}, and Ji​jJ_{ij} that best approximate the function. Mathematically, we aim to minimize the weighted sum of squared residuals:

minθ⁡‖T⁡(A​θ−Y)‖2\min_{\theta}\left\|T(A\theta-Y)\right\|_{2}

Where:

  • •

    θ=[c0,l1,l2,…,lN,J11,J12,…,JN​N]\theta=[c_{0},l_{1},l_{2},\dots,l_{N},J_{11},J_{12},\dots,J_{NN}] represents the vector of coefficients (parameters).

  • •

    YY is the vector of actual values {log⁡ρvv​(v(i))}\{\log\rho_{v}^{v}(v^{(i)})\} for the sample set {v(i)}\{v^{(i)}\}.

  • •

    TT is a diagonal weight matrix, where Ti​i=ρvv​(v(i))T_{ii}=\rho_{v}^{v}(v^{(i)}).

The matrix AA is the design matrix that contains the constant, linear, and quadratic terms. Its structure is:

A=[1v1(1)v2(1)…vN(1)(v1(1))2v1(1)​v2(1)…(vN(1))21v1(2)v2(2)…vN(2)(v1(2))2v1(2)​v2(2)…(vN(2))21v1(k)v2(k)…vN(k)(v1(k))2v1(k)​v2(k)…(vN(k))2]A=\begin{bmatrix}1&v_{1}^{(1)}&v_{2}^{(1)}&\dots&v_{N}^{(1)}&(v_{1}^{(1)})^{2}&v_{1}^{(1)}v_{2}^{(1)}&\dots&(v_{N}^{(1)})^{2}\\ 1&v_{1}^{(2)}&v_{2}^{(2)}&\dots&v_{N}^{(2)}&(v_{1}^{(2)})^{2}&v_{1}^{(2)}v_{2}^{(2)}&\dots&(v_{N}^{(2)})^{2}\\ \vdots&\vdots&\vdots&\vdots&\vdots&\vdots&\vdots&\vdots\\ 1&v_{1}^{(k)}&v_{2}^{(k)}&\dots&v_{N}^{(k)}&(v_{1}^{(k)})^{2}&v_{1}^{(k)}v_{2}^{(k)}&\dots&(v_{N}^{(k)})^{2}\\ \end{bmatrix}

The solution to this problem is given by:

θ=(AT​T​A)−1​AT​T​Y\theta=(A^{T}TA)^{-1}A^{T}TY

Non-linear fitting: The optimal values for the parameters θ={c0,li,Ji​j}\theta=\{c_{0},l_{i},J_{ij}\}, obtained from the preceding least-squares optimization, serve as a starting point for the non-linear optimization procedure. This step refines the parameter estimates by directly minimizing the difference between the distributions, yielding more accurate results, in contrast to the previous step, where the logarithms of the distributions were compared.

The cost function for this optimization is defined as:

C=minθ⁡‖exp⁡(Pk​(θ,v))−ρvv​(v)‖2C=\min_{\theta}\left\|\exp(P_{k}(\theta,v))-\rho_{v}^{v}(v)\right\|_{2}

where exp⁡(Pk​(θ,v))\exp(P_{k}(\theta,v)) represents the approximate probability distribution represented by the exponential of the Polynomial dependent on the parameters θ\theta, and ρvv​(v)\rho_{v}^{v}(v) is the target distribution. The goal is to minimize the L2L_{2}-norm of the difference between these distributions. In our work, we employ the BFGS algorithm, a quasi-Newton optimization method, to minimize the cost function. BFGS uses both gradient information and an approximation of the Hessian matrix to guide the search for the optimal parameters. Gradients are approximated using finite differences, allowing BFGS to iteratively refine the parameters despite the absence of explicit derivatives. The result of the non-linear fitting provides the optimal values for the parameters c0c_{0}, lil_{i}, and Ji​jJ_{ij}. These parameters can then be used to construct the values of ϕv​(X→)\phi_{v}(\vec{X}) for any given configuration vv.

In this section, we derive the gradient expressions for the state ansatz with respect to its parameters. These gradients are crucial for training the model parameters. We provide analytical forms for the gradient of the density matrix and the expectation value of observables.

Appendix F Quantum Circuits

The sampling circuit for quantum proposals requires a kk-qubit generalization of the Rz​zR_{zz} gate, denoted as Rz​z​z​…​zR_{zzz\ldots z}. Here, kk represents the order of interactions allowed in the surrogate network, with Rz​z​z​…​zR_{zzz\ldots z} acting on kk-qubits. This section outlines two methods to implement these gates using different kinds of two-qubit entangling gates along with arbitrary single-qubit unitary gates.

CNOT gate + arbitrary single qubit unitary operations : The first approach utilizes a gate set composed of the CNOT gate and arbitrary single-qubit rotations. The decomposition of the Rz​z​z​…​zR_{zzz\ldots z} gate into this gate set is as follows:

Rz​z​z..z​(θ)=∏i=0k−2C​N​O​T​(i,i+1)​Rzk​(θ)​∏i=k−20C​N​O​T​(i,i+1)R_{zzz..z}(\theta)=\prod_{i=0}^{k-2}CNOT(i,i+1)\;\;R_{z}^{k}(\theta)\;\;\prod_{i=k-2}^{0}CNOT(i,i+1)

where the CNOT gates create the necessary entanglement structure, and the Rzk​(θ)R_{z}^{k}(\theta) gate applies the z-rotation on the kk-th qubit. This decomposition is depicted in Figure 7.

Echoed Cross-Resonance (ECR) gate + arbitrary single qubit unitary operations: An alternative implementation of the Rz​z​z​…​zR_{zzz\ldots z} gate utilizes the Echoed Cross-Resonance (ECR) gate as the two-qubit entangling operation, combined with arbitrary single-qubit rotations. The ECR gate is functionally equivalent to the CNOT gate, differing only by additional single-qubit rotations. However, they are typically preferred over CNOT gates as they are native interactions in certain quantum architectures and often exhibit lower error rates.

A known relationship between the CNOT and ECR gates allows us to express the Rz​z​z​…​zR_{zzz\ldots z} gate in terms of ECR gates[160]. Specifically, the relation is:

CNOT=[RZ(−π/2)⊗RZ(−π)XRZ(−π)]ECR[X⊗I],\text{CNOT}=\left[R_{Z}(-\pi/2)\otimes R_{Z}(-\pi)\,\sqrt{X}\,R_{Z}(-\pi)\right]\,\text{ECR}\,\left[X\otimes I\right],

where RZ​(θ)R_{Z}(\theta), X\sqrt{X}, and XX are single-qubit operations. This relation neglects a global phase of π/2\pi/2. Using this equivalence, the Rz​z​z​…​zR_{zzz\ldots z} gate can be decomposed into a sequence of ECR gates and arbitrary single-qubit rotations. The decomposition is illustrated in Figure 8.

U​3​(θ,ϕ,λ)=(cos⁡θ2−ei​λ​sin⁡θ2ei​ϕ​sin⁡θ2ei⁡(ϕ+λ)​cos⁡θ2)U3(\theta,\phi,\lambda)=\begin{pmatrix}\cos\frac{\theta}{2}&-e^{i\lambda}\sin\frac{\theta}{2}\\ e^{i\phi}\sin\frac{\theta}{2}&e^{i(\phi+\lambda)}\cos\frac{\theta}{2}\end{pmatrix} (34)

Implementing the k-qubit Rz​z​z​…​zR_{zzz\ldots z} gates on quantum hardware requires only 2​k2k two-qubit entangling gates. This linear scaling in the number of entangling gates ensures that the circuits remain efficient and practical for hardware implementation, even as kk increases. Additionally, the use of hardware-native gate sets, such as ECR gates, further enhances the performance by minimizing gate overhead and reducing error rates in architectures where these gates are natively supported.
